title: The name at death
hook: when there's only strength for one word, Pure Land Buddhists say a name
tomorrow: why do some families count forty-nine days after a death?

segments.voice: Yesterday, phowa: a Tibetan drill of light, taught by teachers and rehearsed early. Toward the light. But not everyone gets years of training.

When people are badly frightened, a stubbed toe, a skid on ice, a phone call at night, they often say a single word, and it's frequently a name. Mom. A partner's name. God. A name is what's left when the long sentences are gone. Long sentences need breath. A name barely does. So what if all you can manage at the end is one name? A large family of Buddhists, the Pure Land schools, build a whole practice on that.
screen: `A SKID ON ICE.` → `A NAME IS WHAT'S LEFT.` → `ONE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The name is Amida, or Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light. A Pure Land sutra tells of his vows, made long ago: anyone who hears his name and turns to him with sincere trust will be born in his Pure Land, a place where awakening comes easily. Another sutra goes further. Even someone who has done great wrong, if at death a good friend sits with them and helps them say the name, ten times, will be welcomed there. In Japanese the words are Namu Amida Butsu. In Vietnamese, Nam mô A Di Đà Phật. That second one is said in Vietnamese homes when someone dies, when someone is sick, sometimes just on hearing hard news. And families gather at the bedside to say it with the dying, so the last sound they hear is the name. Inside Pure Land Buddhism, teachers weigh the deathbed differently. Some urge saying the name all through life and especially at the end. Shinran, a Japanese teacher, taught that birth in the Pure Land is settled the moment trust arises, so the deathbed isn't what decides. Either way, the name works like a handrail in the dark: you don't need to see the whole staircase to hold on. It's a door kept open by someone else's vow, not by the strength of the one who's dying. And anyone at the bedside can say it with them.
screen: `AMIDA, BOUNDLESS LIGHT.` · `A VOW THAT HOLDS THE NAME.` · `SAID WITH THE DYING.` · `TWO WAYS TO WEIGH THE DEATHBED.` · then, large: `THE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is sick, or someone who has died. If this is your practice, say the name softly for them, Namu Amida Butsu, or Nam mô A Di Đà Phật, on each out-breath. If it isn't, say that person's own name on each out-breath, slowly, with a kind wish.
The name at death: Pure Land Buddhists say Amida's name with the dying, trusting a vow to hold them when their own strength can't.
Pocket line: the name at the end, short enough to say when nothing else is. Day twenty-five, named.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in Japan, China, Vietnam and elsewhere recite Amida's name (the nembutsu) daily; at a deathbed, family and temple members often chant it together with the dying person and keep chanting after death.

original.note: Pali buddhanussati: recollection of the Buddha; nembutsu is the Japanese for this idea.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant that only works if you say it perfectly.

what a scholar hears: the Larger Sukhavativyuha Sutra (the vows, esp. the eighteenth) and the Contemplation Sutra (the lowest grade, ten recitations at death); Honen's and Shinran's schools weigh the deathbed differently.

Amida.meaning: the Buddha of boundless light, Amitabha, at the heart of Pure Land

Pure Land.meaning: Amida's realm, where awakening comes easily; also the schools devoted to him

Namu Amida Butsu.meaning: Japanese: I take refuge in Amida Buddha

Shinran.meaning: a Japanese teacher who founded Jodo Shinshu, True Pure Land

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavativyuha Sutra (Amida's vows; those who hear the name with sincere trust are born in the Pure Land)
Contemplation Sutra (Amitayurdhyana Sutra), the lowest grade of birth: a wrongdoer, helped at death by a good friend, says the name ten times
Shinran's teaching that birth is settled when shinjin (true entrusting) arises, without relying on the deathbed

'A large family of Buddhists' (Pure Land schools) avoids a number; confirm. Vietnamese usage of 'Nam mô A Di Đà Phật' on hearing of a death or sickness: common custom; confirm.
